title: CHANCE uses tumor genomes to prioritize non-cancer drugs with activity in patient-derived cancer cells
summary: CHANCE, a supervised machine-learning model integrating patient-specific coding and non-coding mutations with drug and protein-interaction information, screened 5,197 TCGA/ICGC tumors against 923 FDA-approved non-oncology drugs. For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients. This is patient-specific cell-assay validation, not a treatment-response study in patients.
ai_technology: CHANCE, a supervised gradient-boosted-tree model integrating coding/non-coding variants, protein–protein interaction networks, drug targets and drug-response data
organization: Tianjin Medical University; collaborating Chinese cancer research and clinical institutions

evidence.tested: For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients.
evidence.unknown: Only seven patient-derived samples were tested, from pancreatic or esophageal cancers; at least one prioritized non-oncology drug showed activity in five. This was an ex-vivo drug-sensitivity assay, not clinical treatment, and the study does not establish efficacy, safety, dosing or patient benefit. The 5,197-tumor/923-drug screen is computational prediction; only the small patient-derived subset had experimental validation. Drug-response predictions may include drugs represented in training, as the article notes 149 of 923 screened drugs were in the training data.
evidence.ai_role: Trained on drug-sensitivity measurements from 318 cancer cell lines across 647 drugs, CHANCE maps each patient tumor’s whole-genome mutations to drug-target/pathway features and ranks non-oncology drugs by predicted patient-specific anticancer activity. Investigators used these predictions to select drugs for ex-vivo testing in tumor cells from seven patients; the reported five-patient activity result tests the model’s personalized prioritization.
